Child substance abuse

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The epidemic of substance abuse is spreading to children as young as primary school age...and rehab services are all but completely absent.

Unique Selling Point:
A group of children in Joburg's poor western suburbs paints a picture of socio-economic deprivation that, one can only imagine, is all too common in South Africa. These children, whose ages range from around 14 to 6 and even younger, have been a cause for concern for former resident Meghan Botes for over two years. But despite all her efforts to find suitable rehabilitation treatment for the children and social services support for them at home, she is coming up against brick walls in every direction. It seems there simply are no services available for children under the age of 12, which means these kids are simply falling through the gaps in the system.

UPDATE: One of the children was hit by a car last week while buying glue, and died. This and the pandemic have brought the situation into new sharp relief.

Summary:
Meghan and Kevin Botes started trying to help the children of Bosmont when they moved to the area in 2014. They noticed a group of children begging for food and money. The children were dirty, ill-fed and not attending school. A growing number of the kids were also addicted to glue. It soon became clear that most of them lived in one block of flats, where their parents were unemployed and addicts themselves.

Legally, children must be removed from situations in which they are harmed or neglected, but unless a foster facility is willing to take them, the court can't remove them from their parents' care. Because no foster homes deal with child addiction, they've been left in this situation. Meghan has met with the DSD, who indicate they've been familiar with these children since 2015. She has also tried to get them into rehab but can't find anywhere that will offer it to kids younger than 12. She got one or two older boys into an outpatient programme but it was designed for adolescents and adults, and they soon refused to attend.

One home offered to take the children if they were first detoxed. Having read that glue detox takes around 2 weeks, Meghan raised money to take the children on a two-week camp with their parents' permission. It was a success: the kids were clean for a month, and one girl is still clean over a year later. But when Christmas came most of them relapsed. When Meghan approached DSD for help funding a second camp, she was told she's not a registered NPO and shouldn't run camps. There's also been minimal effort to ensure the kids don't return to the same dysfunctional home environment.

The situation is deadlocked. Meghan is trying to register an NPO to provide rehab, and tries to be a constant presence in the kids' lives by spending Tuesday evenings providing food and a short Bible/prayer session. Meanwhile, nothing is fundamentally changing for the children.

Further information:
“Inhalant” encompasses a wide range of substances that readily vaporize at room temperature, inhaled to achieve an altered state of mind eg euphoria, disinhibition. Glue is also known to reduce feelings of cold and hunger. Inhalants are commonly and disproportionately abused by children from socio-economically disadvantaged communities because they're cheap, easy to acquire and not classed as illegal drugs. Experimentation with inhalants is a risk factor for continued use of illicit drugs later in life and premature death. Inhalants act in ways similar to other drugs, as central nervous system depressants. Health implications include brain malfunction, delirium, brain oedema (fluid build-up and swelling), neuropsychiatric impairment, permanent neurobiological changes, anxiolytic effects, sensory effects, learning, memory and operant behaviour, psychotic disorders, mood disorders, and anxiety disorder. Inhalants are one of a few substances that can cause a long-term consequence of persisting dementia. Motor impairments include Muscle weakness, loss of mobility, atrophy, decreased tendon reflexes, demyelination, alterations in spontaneous motor activity, anticonvulsant effects. Long-term health effects include cardiac toxicity, respiratory problems, kidney problems, hepatitis, bone marrow suppression, and developmental problems in foetuses. Death may be immediate, due to sudden sniffing death, suffocation, aspiration, trauma, drowning, or fire - or delayed, due to cardiomyopathy, central nervous system toxicity, aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, renal toxicity, etc.

There is minimal research on the topic worldwide, especially on child inhalant abuse, and effective treatment. Most clinicians rely on methods that are used to treat other addictive disorders, such as cognitive-behavioural therapy, multi system and family therapy, 12-step facilitation, and motivational enhancement therapy. Patients can detox with 2-4 weeks therapy and see cognitive improvements within 6 weeks. Some deficits improve more slowly over months and years; some are never recovered. Older and chronic users have less improvement. Challenges to treatment include poly-substance abuse and comorbidity. Outcomes are self-reported, recovery is slow and variable, and the effects continue after discontinuation. Inhalants are often not targeted in drug education programmes because they are seen as more harmless than illicit drugs, and sale to children is not restricted.

The problem of children under 12 years abusing inhalants is essentially invisible in SA because the data we have on drug abuse comes from treatment centres. Since children this young generally don't access these services, they don't appear in the stats and some DSD officials have been known to say the problem simply doesn't exist. The MRC's South African Community Epidemiology Network on Drug Use nevertheless does have a few instances of children as young as 8 years old receiving drug rehab therapy. According to a 2016 report, in the Western Cape, school children were the second largest group of patients, with around 5% aged 10-14, although only 1 patient was admitted for inhalant abuse in the period under review. In the same period, in Gauteng, less than 1% of patients were under 10, with around 2-3% aged 10-14. The same report says “Patients treated for inhalants were the youngest on average”.

Script:


UPSOUND: ‘Anastasia’: You put it in a packet and you suck it and you smoke. And when it hits you then you feel nothing.
LINK1: This is a suburb in the west, near the inner city of Joburg. The community here is poor, many are unemployed, and substance abuse is common. But what is unexpected and shocking is the tender age of some of those that are addicted.
UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: Why do you sniff glue?
‘Elton’: Because I saw it by other friends and I also learned how to smoke it.
VO1: Elton and Anastasia (not their real names) are both 12 years old. They have both been inhaling glue for about three years. A drawn-out search for help has yielded very little hope.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: This is where we lived when we just got married and this is where the children would come almost every day.
VO2: Nurse educator Meghan Botes and her husband were horrified when they realised the young children who begged at their door were addicted to glue.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: As the years progressed they got older but the younger siblings joined in. So their ages at the moment range from about 6 to 13.
LINK2: Glue is an inhalant – a substance that is sniffed to create a high. It’s often abused by children, because it’s not illegal or age-restricted – in fact, it’s cheap and readily available.
UPSOUND: Anastasia: We go beg here then we go buy it.
Macfarlane Moleli: You go beg. And then how much does it cost?
Anastasia: Thirteen rand. And fifteen.
Macfarlane Moleli: Thirteen rand. For a small bottle like that.
Anastasia: Yes and for a big bottle it’s twenty rand.
UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: Meghan, do you know why they choose to use glue?
Meghan Botes: Besides the hallucination effect which isn't always present in all of them, it also suppresses cold and hunger. So for children who are not often fed well or not dressed well in the cold or at night, it helps. I mean, some of the things that we've seen are dreadful, where the older child is left to look after the baby and because the baby won't stop crying, they share their glue.
UPSOUND: Rebecca Coetzee: Cognitively, emotionally, spiritually, a lot of the basic needs are not even supplied. They are learning different strategies to fulfil their own needs.
VO3: Psychiatric nurse Rebecca Coetzee has joined Meghan in seeking a solution for these children.
UPSOUND: Rebecca Coetzee: With their immature systems, it actually can stunt their growth and it can affect their cognitive abilities. If you've already damaged your brain at the age of six, your prognosis is not that great.
LINK3: Experimenting with inhalants is a risk factor for illicit drug use later in life, and for premature death. The danger was tragically illustrated on this road just a few weeks ago.
VO4: The children were begging for money and gambling on the side of a busy main road, when an 11 year-old boy was hit by a car.
UPSOUND: Elton: He landed on his face. He was still moving a little bit. We ran to go tell his mother what happened and when we came back, he was closed with foil.
UPSOUND: ‘Simone’: When I came there he was already dead.
VO5: The boy’s mother – we’ll call her Simone – is an unemployed single parent who struggles with addiction herself.
UPSOUND: Simone: I was hitting him every day. But the more I hit him the more he go out with friends and they’ll go the whole day.
UPSOUND: Rebecca Coetzee: What made me more sad is that we weren't able to help him before he actually passed on.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: We've tried every avenue we possibly could.
VO6: The biggest stumbling block is the sheer youth of these addicts.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: NGO, NPO, private, government - we could not find an inpatient rehabilitation centre for children under twelve anywhere.
UPSOUND: Adrie Vermeulen: We are constantly realizing that our age group is becoming younger. If we look at our statistics, the mean age of experimenting with substances is 12.
VO7: Adrie Vermeulen is the national coordinator for SANCA, a network of about 30 NGOs focused on substance abuse. She says SANCA has only 6 inpatient rehab centres for children. Of those, only one has recently been re-registered to admit children from age 10; the rest are registered for teenagers.
UPSOUND: Adrie Vermeulen: It's not enough. When you start looking at the younger ones we need specialist treatment services for them.
VO8: Although there is no lower age limit for outpatient programmes, here children are treated alongside teenagers.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: So you go once a week and then you go home and you’re expected to stay off the glue by yourself. And they gave them like, you know, information leaflets but they can't really read. So it wasn't appropriate.
VO9: Last year, the Gauteng Department of Social Development acknowledged to Meghan that they’d been aware of these children for some time.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: The social workers say they tried to remove the children but they couldn't because first of all the children run away when they see the social workers coming. And secondly the parents swear at the social workers and they don't feel safe.
VO10: In a written comment, the Department told us these cases were reported in 2018, and agreed the children were in need of care and protection. It said it has attempted to intervene several times, including a temporary removal, and referral to outpatient programmes and psychological services. The children under 12 were then referred to the NPO, Joburg Child Welfare. Joburg Child Welfare told us they have tried numerous times to remove the children and place them in care facilities, but have failed, largely due to opposition from the children’s parents, including verbal abuse and death threats. They told us they don’t have the specialist knowledge to run Rehabilitation Centres, and instead refer cases of substance abuse to SANCA….even though SANCA doesn’t cater for children this young.
UPSOUND: Karabo Ozah: Section 28(1)(c) of the Constitution says that children are entitled to parental care, family care, but where all those fail, then state care.
VO12: Director of the Centre for Child Law, Karabo Ozah, says when children are exposed to harm, the Children’s Act requires the state to step in and, if necessary, remove them from their parents’ care.
UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: Is it possible for anyone to make the argument that these children are refusing rehab and they have a right to do that?
Karabo Ozah: Well, no. They are children in need of care and protection. And you don’t need consent – their consent – to assist them. You have that obligation as the state.
VO13: She says the law requires the Department of Social Development to provide substance abuse programmes for all children under 18.
UPSOUND: Karabo Ozah: And I think people must be taken to task and must be made to do their work. You can’t have also children hanging because we say there’s no facility. That is totally wrong.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: If they put them into a children's home, they're going to overwhelm that home. They need to be in a place where there’s someone that understands the fact that they are addicted and not going to treat them like naughty children.
VO14: In September last year, Meghan met with Gauteng DSD leadership, who suggested she register her own rehab programme.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: It requires a lot of time. And this specific group of children don't have time. So we gave them a list of names. And they promised us that they would investigate those specific cases. And since that meeting last year they have not replied to one of my emails.
VO15: The little boy who died was on that list. The Department said Meghan was aware that Joburg Child Welfare was assisting the children. Joburg Child Welfare said that the COVID-19 lockdown had prevented follow-up on the cases this year.
UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: Do you miss him?
Elton: Yes uncle, he was my best friend.
VO16: Since his death, five of his cousins, all over age 10, have been removed and placed in a SANCA facility.
UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: that might be some sort of ray of light?
Adrie Vermeulen: Yes, I think that's a ray of light and it's the first step. After treatment, you know, that's where the real challenge starts happening. Our concern is that we place those children right back into the midst of the war.
LINK5: While some of the children may finally be getting the help they need, the rest, and many like them, continue to simply fall through the cracks – until they turn 18 and lose the protection of the Children’s Act.
UPSOUND: Karabo Ozah: When we’re not intervening, we’re failing them. We’re failing the children and it means that in future we’re going to have this group of adults who we failed as children, who now have these serious problems because when we could intervene earlier, we failed to do so.
VO17: The Department said it has referred the families for skills development and substance abuse treatment. Joburg Child Welfare said that broader intervention was “almost impossible in the atmosphere of conflict and mistrust”.
Meghan and Rebecca have applied to register an NPO and continue to do what they can for the kids.
UPSOUND: Rebecca Coetzee: We made the decision that we just want to be consistent caring adults in their lives.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: We decided that we'd go weekly to see the children, to have a short program, give out sandwiches, just touch base with them.
UPSOUND: Rebecca Coetzee: It's actually so much fun spending time with them and getting to know them.
UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: Inside of them there's a normal child that wants to play and feel safe.
UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: If I gave you a hundred thousand rand, what would you do to change your life?
Elton: Buy groceries uncle.
Macfarlane Moleli: So much food!
Elton: Yes uncle. For a whole year uncle. Two years uncle.

PROMOS

1. You may think substance abuse is the domain of adults… but in these Johannesburg streets, younger and younger children are the addicts, and glue is the drug of choice.


2. We go inside a Johannesburg suburb where children as young as six are addicted to glue. When rehab programmes are virtually non-existent, what can be done to give these children a future?


3. In this Johannesburg suburb, glue is the drug of choice for children as young as six. Community members have spent years battling to help these children recover from their devastating addiction.

He was still moving a little bit. We ran to go tell his mother what happened and when we came back, he was closed with foil. UPSOUND: ‘Simone’: When I came there he was already dead. VO5: The boy’s mother – we’ll call her Simone – is an unemployed single parent who struggles with addiction herself. UPSOUND: Simone: I was hitting him every day. But the more I hit him the more he go out with friends and they’ll go the whole day. UPSOUND: Rebecca Coetzee: What made me more sad is that we weren't able to help him before he actually passed on. UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: We've tried every avenue we possibly could. VO6: The biggest stumbling block is the sheer youth of these addicts. UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: NGO, NPO, private, government - we could not find an inpatient rehabilitation centre for children under twelve anywhere. UPSOUND: Adrie Vermeulen: We are constantly realizing that our age group is becoming younger. If we look at our statistics, the mean age of experimenting with substances is 12. VO7: Adrie Vermeulen is the national coordinator for SANCA, a network of about 30 NGOs focused on substance abuse. She says SANCA has only 6 inpatient rehab centres for children. Of those, only one has recently been re-registered to admit children from age 10; the rest are registered for teenagers. UPSOUND: Adrie Vermeulen: It's not enough. When you start looking at the younger ones we need specialist treatment services for them. VO8: Although there is no lower age limit for outpatient programmes, here children are treated alongside teenagers. UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: So you go once a week and then you go home and you’re expected to stay off the glue by yourself. And they gave them like, you know, information leaflets but they can't really read. So it wasn't appropriate. VO9: Last year, the Gauteng Department of Social Development acknowledged to Meghan that they’d been aware of these children for some time. UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: The social workers say they tried to remove the children but they couldn't because first of all the children run away when they see the social workers coming. And secondly the parents swear at the social workers and they don't feel safe. VO10: In a written comment, the Department told us these cases were reported in 2018, and agreed the children were in need of care and protection. It said it has attempted to intervene several times, including a temporary removal, and referral to outpatient programmes and psychological services. The children under 12 were then referred to the NPO, Joburg Child Welfare. Joburg Child Welfare told us they have tried numerous times to remove the children and place them in care facilities, but have failed, largely due to opposition from the children’s parents, including verbal abuse and death threats. They told us they don’t have the specialist knowledge to run Rehabilitation Centres, and instead refer cases of substance abuse to SANCA….even though SANCA doesn’t cater for children this young. UPSOUND: Karabo Ozah: Section 28(1)(c) of the Constitution says that children are entitled to parental care, family care, but where all those fail, then state care. VO12: Director of the Centre for Child Law, Karabo Ozah, says when children are exposed to harm, the Children’s Act requires the state to step in and, if necessary, remove them from their parents’ care. UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: Is it possible for anyone to make the argument that these children are refusing rehab and they have a right to do that? Karabo Ozah: Well, no. They are children in need of care and protection. And you don’t need consent – their consent – to assist them. You have that obligation as the state. VO13: She says the law requires the Department of Social Development to provide substance abuse programmes for all children under 18. UPSOUND: Karabo Ozah: And I think people must be taken to task and must be made to do their work. You can’t have also children hanging because we say there’s no facility. That is totally wrong. UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: If they put them into a children's home, they're going to overwhelm that home. They need to be in a place where there’s someone that understands the fact that they are addicted and not going to treat them like naughty children. VO14: In September last year, Meghan met with Gauteng DSD leadership, who suggested she register her own rehab programme. UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: It requires a lot of time. And this specific group of children don't have time. So we gave them a list of names. And they promised us that they would investigate those specific cases. And since that meeting last year they have not replied to one of my emails. VO15: The little boy who died was on that list. The Department said Meghan was aware that Joburg Child Welfare was assisting the children. Joburg Child Welfare said that the COVID-19 lockdown had prevented follow-up on the cases this year. UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: Do you miss him? Elton: Yes uncle, he was my best friend. VO16: Since his death, five of his cousins, all over age 10, have been removed and placed in a SANCA facility. UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: that might be some sort of ray of light? Adrie Vermeulen: Yes, I think that's a ray of light and it's the first step. After treatment, you know, that's where the real challenge starts happening. Our concern is that we place those children right back into the midst of the war. LINK5: While some of the children may finally be getting the help they need, the rest, and many like them, continue to simply fall through the cracks – until they turn 18 and lose the protection of the Children’s Act. UPSOUND: Karabo Ozah: When we’re not intervening, we’re failing them. We’re failing the children and it means that in future we’re going to have this group of adults who we failed as children, who now have these serious problems because when we could intervene earlier, we failed to do so. VO17: The Department said it has referred the families for skills development and substance abuse treatment. Joburg Child Welfare said that broader intervention was “almost impossible in the atmosphere of conflict and mistrust”. Meghan and Rebecca have applied to register an NPO and continue to do what they can for the kids. UPSOUND: Rebecca Coetzee: We made the decision that we just want to be consistent caring adults in their lives. UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: We decided that we'd go weekly to see the children, to have a short program, give out sandwiches, just touch base with them. UPSOUND: Rebecca Coetzee: It's actually so much fun spending time with them and getting to know them. UPSOUND: Meghan Botes: Inside of them there's a normal child that wants to play and feel safe. UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: If I gave you a hundred thousand rand, what would you do to change your life? Elton: Buy groceries uncle. Macfarlane Moleli: So much food! Elton: Yes uncle. For a whole year uncle. Two years uncle. PROMOS 1. You may think substance abuse is the domain of adults… but in these Johannesburg streets, younger and younger children are the addicts, and glue is the drug of choice. 2. We go inside a Johannesburg suburb where children as young as six are addicted to glue. When rehab programmes are virtually non-existent, what can be done to give these children a future? 3. In this Johannesburg suburb, glue is the drug of choice for children as young as six. Community members have spent years battling to help these children recover from their devastating addiction.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The epidemic of substance abuse is spreading to children as young as primary school age...and rehab services are all but completely absent.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A group of children in Joburg's poor western suburbs paints a picture of socio-economic deprivation that, one can only imagine, is all too common in South Africa. These children, whose ages range from around 14 to 6 and even younger, have been a cause for concern for former resident Meghan Botes for over two years. But despite all her efforts to find suitable rehabilitation treatment for the children and social services support for them at home, she is coming up against brick walls in every direction. It seems there simply are no services available for children under the age of 12, which means these kids are simply falling through the gaps in the system. UPDATE: One of the children was hit by a car last week while buying glue, and died. This and the pandemic have brought the situation into new sharp relief.
metadata.Summary: Meghan and Kevin Botes started trying to help the children of Bosmont when they moved to the area in 2014. They noticed a group of children begging for food and money. The children were dirty, ill-fed and not attending school. A growing number of the kids were also addicted to glue. It soon became clear that most of them lived in one block of flats, where their parents were unemployed and addicts themselves. Legally, children must be removed from situations in which they are harmed or neglected, but unless a foster facility is willing to take them, the court can't remove them from their parents' care. Because no foster homes deal with child addiction, they've been left in this situation. Meghan has met with the DSD, who indicate they've been familiar with these children since 2015. She has also tried to get them into rehab but can't find anywhere that will offer it to kids younger than 12. She got one or two older boys into an outpatient programme but it was designed for adolescents and adults, and they soon refused to attend. One home offered to take the children if they were first detoxed. Having read that glue detox takes around 2 weeks, Meghan raised money to take the children on a two-week camp with their parents' permission. It was a success: the kids were clean for a month, and one girl is still clean over a year later. But when Christmas came most of them relapsed. When Meghan approached DSD for help funding a second camp, she was told she's not a registered NPO and shouldn't run camps. There's also been minimal effort to ensure the kids don't return to the same dysfunctional home environment. The situation is deadlocked. Meghan is trying to register an NPO to provide rehab, and tries to be a constant presence in the kids' lives by spending Tuesday evenings providing food and a short Bible/prayer session. Meanwhile, nothing is fundamentally changing for the children.
metadata.Further information: “Inhalant” encompasses a wide range of substances that readily vaporize at room temperature, inhaled to achieve an altered state of mind eg euphoria, disinhibition. Glue is also known to reduce feelings of cold and hunger. Inhalants are commonly and disproportionately abused by children from socio-economically disadvantaged communities because they're cheap, easy to acquire and not classed as illegal drugs. Experimentation with inhalants is a risk factor for continued use of illicit drugs later in life and premature death. Inhalants act in ways similar to other drugs, as central nervous system depressants. Health implications include brain malfunction, delirium, brain oedema (fluid build-up and swelling), neuropsychiatric impairment, permanent neurobiological changes, anxiolytic effects, sensory effects, learning, memory and operant behaviour, psychotic disorders, mood disorders, and anxiety disorder. Inhalants are one of a few substances that can cause a long-term consequence of persisting dementia. Motor impairments include Muscle weakness, loss of mobility, atrophy, decreased tendon reflexes, demyelination, alterations in spontaneous motor activity, anticonvulsant effects. Long-term health effects include cardiac toxicity, respiratory problems, kidney problems, hepatitis, bone marrow suppression, and developmental problems in foetuses. Death may be immediate, due to sudden sniffing death, suffocation, aspiration, trauma, drowning, or fire - or delayed, due to cardiomyopathy, central nervous system toxicity, aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, renal toxicity, etc. There is minimal research on the topic worldwide, especially on child inhalant abuse, and effective treatment. Most clinicians rely on methods that are used to treat other addictive disorders, such as cognitive-behavioural therapy, multi system and family therapy, 12-step facilitation, and motivational enhancement therapy. Patients can detox with 2-4 weeks therapy and see cognitive improvements within 6 weeks. Some deficits improve more slowly over months and years; some are never recovered. Older and chronic users have less improvement. Challenges to treatment include poly-substance abuse and comorbidity. Outcomes are self-reported, recovery is slow and variable, and the effects continue after discontinuation. Inhalants are often not targeted in drug education programmes because they are seen as more harmless than illicit drugs, and sale to children is not restricted. The problem of children under 12 years abusing inhalants is essentially invisible in SA because the data we have on drug abuse comes from treatment centres. Since children this young generally don't access these services, they don't appear in the stats and some DSD officials have been known to say the problem simply doesn't exist. The MRC's South African Community Epidemiology Network on Drug Use nevertheless does have a few instances of children as young as 8 years old receiving drug rehab therapy. According to a 2016 report, in the Western Cape, school children were the second largest group of patients, with around 5% aged 10-14, although only 1 patient was admitted for inhalant abuse in the period under review. In the same period, in Gauteng, less than 1% of patients were under 10, with around 2-3% aged 10-14. The same report says “Patients treated for inhalants were the youngest on average”.
